evidence_base.sufficiency_note: 17 sessions across 8 months and 6 subjects supports a genuine profile, including which patterns are habitual versus one-off.

cognitive_types.label: Fluency
cognitive_types.definition: Retrieving or recalling known material fast and automatically
cognitive_types.summary: Deliberate self-quizzing on organelles, vocabulary and DNA replication enzymes — confident recall, and one real-time self-correction on a recurring mix-up.

snippets.subject: Science

preceding_ai_turn.text: What's in a plant cell that's not in an animal cell?

student_turn.text: cell wall, chloroplast, and a big vacuole. animal cells have small vacuoles or none

snippets.why: Confident, correct recall across a full self-drilled quiz round before a test.

snippets.subject: Science

preceding_ai_turn.text: Close — that's the one that builds the new strand. The one that unzips it is helicase.

student_turn.text: oh right i always mix those two up

snippets.why: Names his own recurring mix-up by name rather than just accepting the correction and moving on.

cognitive_types.label: Procedural
cognitive_types.definition: Executing a known sequence correctly, step by step
cognitive_types.summary: Reliable once he's caught up on content — shows his own work, applies newly reconstructed rules correctly, and once catches and fixes his own procedural error mid-answer.

snippets.subject: Science

preceding_ai_turn.text: Good catch stopping yourself — you're right that WW doesn't reappear the same way. In incomplete dominance there's no W allele at all, just R and a different allele, call it R'. Rr is really RR' here. Want to redo it with that fixed?

student_turn.text: yeah so RR' x RR' — 1 RR red, 2 RR' pink, 1 R'R' white. 1:2:1 phenotype same as genotype since none of them are fully dominant

snippets.why: Re-executes the cross correctly immediately after catching his own model error, with the reasoning visible in his own words.

snippets.subject: Mathematics

preceding_ai_turn.text: A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One of the angles formed measures 65°. Find the corresponding angle, the alternate interior angle, and the co-interior angle at the other intersection.

student_turn.text: corresponding would be 65, alternate interior would also be 65, and co-interior would be 115 since 180-65

snippets.why: Applies three angle relationships correctly to a new problem right after reconstructing them himself.

cognitive_types.label: Conceptual
cognitive_types.definition: Building or repairing a mental model of how something works
cognitive_types.summary: His clearest strength when he's caught up on missed content — rebuilds why a process works, not just what it does, and predicts unstated relationships before being told them.

snippets.subject: Science

preceding_ai_turn.text: Correct. So why does meiosis need to make 4 instead of 2 — what's it for that mitosis isn't?

student_turn.text: growing/repairing vs making eggs and sperm. so meiosis has to cut the chromosome number in half so when they combine it goes back to normal

snippets.why: States the actual causal reason meiosis halves the chromosome count, not just the fact that it does — his own model, externalized.

snippets.subject: Mathematics

preceding_ai_turn.text: Correct. One more — co-interior, also called same-side interior. Any guess what's true about those, given the other two are both equal?

student_turn.text: if the other ones are equal maybe these add up to something instead. 180?

snippets.why: Predicts an unstated angle relationship by reasoning from the two he already has, rather than asking for it.

cognitive_types.label: Critical Thinking
cognitive_types.definition: Evaluating, reasoning about, or challenging a claim
cognitive_types.summary: Appears once in the corpus, in a DBQ source-evaluation session, and is fully realized when it does — he builds his own method for weighing two self-interested sources against each other.

snippets.subject: Social Studies

preceding_ai_turn.text: Right. So neither is neutral. Does that mean you can't use either one?

student_turn.text: no i think you can still use both, you just gotta say why each one might be slanted. like use the newspaper for what actually happened logistically but not for who to blame

snippets.why: Builds his own method for using biased sources — separating factual claims from interpretive ones — instead of picking a side or discarding both.

cognitive_types.label: Creative
cognitive_types.definition: Generating something novel; diverging rather than converging
cognitive_types.summary: Strong both times it appears, and only after the tutor declined to just generate for him — a fully self-designed studio art piece, and a self-written essay opening line.

snippets.subject: Visual Arts

preceding_ai_turn.text: Do you want to work in a medium that can hold stillness, or do you want movement in it somehow — light changing, steam from something?

student_turn.text: steam. like from the kettle. that could be the one moving thing in a still picture

snippets.why: Supplies the piece's entire original concept himself — subject, mood, and the one deliberate motion in an otherwise still image.

snippets.subject: English

preceding_ai_turn.text: That's your thesis, basically — a shift from expecting things to be handled to just handling them. Want to try writing the first two sentences yourself, and I'll tell you honestly if they land?

student_turn.text: ok. 'nobody told me the morning was mine now. it just was, one day, and i had to figure out what that meant.'

snippets.why: Writes an original opening line himself, after the tutor declined his initial request to write the paragraph for him.

cognitive_types.label: Metacognitive
cognitive_types.definition: Monitoring and regulating their own thinking and learning
cognitive_types.summary: The most frequent type in the transcript — he plans ahead of absences instead of just reacting to them, and once diagnoses on his own that three behind subjects need three different kinds of catch-up.

snippets.subject: Study Skills

preceding_ai_turn.text: Which three, and for each one — is the problem that you don't understand the material, or that you haven't seen enough of it yet?

student_turn.text: bio and geometry i think i understand it when i catch up, its history where i actually dont get some of it, not just missed days

snippets.why: Diagnoses that his three behind subjects need different kinds of help before being told, and is specific about which is a content gap versus an understanding gap.

snippets.subject: Mathematics

student_turn.text: what did geometry cover today, im not going to be there

snippets.why: Proactively asks what he'll miss before an absence happens, instead of catching up after the fact.

cognitive_types.label: Transfer
cognitive_types.definition: Applying something known to a genuinely different context
cognitive_types.summary: Appears once, in May, and is fully realized — he notices unprompted that a geometry proof and a history source-evaluation method share the same underlying structure, and extends the pattern to how he checks his own biology work.

snippets.subject: Mathematics

preceding_ai_turn.text: Say more about that — what's the structural similarity you're seeing?

student_turn.text: like in the proof you use two different facts (alternate angles and corresponding angles) that both independently prove the lines are parallel. and with the history documents, two sources that disagree on blame still both independently confirmed the same date and injuries. its like using two paths to the same answer to make it more solid

snippets.why: Recognizes the same 'independent lines of evidence' structure under two completely different surfaces, unprompted, and later extends it to a third (checking his own biology answers).

cognitive_types.label: Exploratory
cognitive_types.definition: Encountering new information and taking it in
cognitive_types.summary: No session in this corpus is open-ended or curiosity-driven; every one is tied to an assignment, a test, or an absence.

offloading.summary: One clean offload in the whole corpus, isolated to a single evening and a single class, under real time pressure the night before a test.

instances.subject: Social Studies

student_turn.text: i really dont have time tonight, my night got messed up. can u just give me all of them

instances.note: He had worked most of the study guide himself and had three sections left the night before the test. When the tutor offered to scaffold the first answer so he could find the pattern, he said there wasn't time and asked for everything, which the tutor then gave. He copied it down with no follow-up questions. His History unit exam three days later (2026-03-19) was his lowest score of the school year.

teacher_actions.action: Deshawn doesn't get open-ended, curiosity-driven time with the tutor — every session is assignment- or catch-up-driven. On a lighter week, point him at one no-stakes 'just curious' question with no due date attached, in a subject he isn't behind in.
teacher_actions.rationale: All 17 sessions are tied to an assignment, a test, or an absence; the profile has no exploratory sessions at all. That likely reflects how little slack his schedule has rather than a lack of curiosity — his Studio Art and Transfer sessions show real range whenever he has the room for it.

teacher_actions.action: Watch for the pattern from 2026-03-16: under real time pressure the night before a History test, he asked for and got a full set of study-guide answers with no follow-up, and his score on that unit exam (79) was his lowest of the year. A standing 'flag it by Wednesday, not the night before' check-in for that class specifically could catch the next one before it happens.
teacher_actions.rationale: This is the one clean offload in the whole corpus, it's isolated to a single class, and it lines up with a real dip in that subject's exam score three days later.

teacher_actions.action: He already invented a real study strategy on his own (2025-12-15 — different methods for different subjects, cause-and-effect chains for history specifically) and a scheduling fix for his make-up tests (2026-02-23 — asking for a before-school slot instead of losing lunch). Ask him directly, once, whether either is still working — he isn't likely to bring it up unprompted.
teacher_actions.rationale: Both are self-generated, practical fixes to real constraints in his day, and the kind of thing that's easy to miss because he never announces it — he just does it.

teacher_actions.action: He made a genuine cross-subject connection unprompted in May — geometry proofs and historical source evaluation share the same 'independent lines of evidence' structure — and extended it to how he checks his own biology work. Ask him, roughly monthly, whether something from one class reminds him of another.
teacher_actions.rationale: Transfer appeared exactly once in 17 sessions but was fully realized when it did, the same 'proven capability, not yet a habit' pattern that's worth deliberately cultivating.

caveats: This is one AI tutor on one platform across one school year — it doesn't capture in-class work, paper homework, tests, or conversations with teachers and peers.

Sessions are self-selected: he brought these conversations to the tutor, almost always early morning before school or in the library in the afternoon, which skews the sample toward catch-up and homework-shaped tasks rather than however he engages with material when he isn't behind.
Depth ratings reflect what he wrote in the moment, not independently verified retention.
The single offloading instance is real but isolated to one evening and one subject — one instance in 17 sessions is a flagged event, not yet a demonstrated pattern.
